results.content: Candès∗† Pragya Sur∗ April 27, 2018 Abstract This paper rigorously establishes that the existence of the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) in high-dimensional logistic regression models with Gaussian covariates undergoes a sharp ‘phase transition’. We introduce an explicit boundary curve hMLE, parameterized by two scalars measuring the overall magnitude of the unknown sequence of regression coeﬃcients, with the following property: in the limit of large sample sizes n and number of features p proportioned in such a way that p/n →κ, we show that if the problem is suﬃciently high dimensional in the sense that κ > hMLE, then the MLE does not exist with probability one. For instance, every statistician knows that if the n data points (xi, yi) are completely separated in the sense that that there is a linear decision boundary parameterized by b ∈Rp with the property yix′ ib > 0, for all i, (1) then the MLE does not exist. When applied to logistic regression, Cover’s 2 main result states the following: assume that the xi’s are drawn i.i.d. from a distribution F obeying some speciﬁc assumptions and that the class labels are independent from xi and have equal marginal probabilities; i.e. P(yi = 1|xi) = 1/2. Hence, the results from [5,6] and [17] describe a phase transition in the existence of the MLE as the dimensionality parameter κ = p/n varies around the value 1/2. We prove that the transition occurs in an interval of width O(n−1/2): take any sequence λn →∞; then p/n > hMLE(β0, γ0) + λnn−1/2 = ⇒ limn,p→∞P{MLE exists} = 0, p/n < hMLE(β0, γ0) −λnn−1/2 = ⇒ limn,p→∞P{MLE exists} = 1. Below, each simulated data set follows a logistic model with n = 4, 000, p = κ n, i.i.d. Gaussian covariates with identity covariance matrix (note that our results do not depend on the covariance Σ) and β selected appropriately so that Var(x′ iβ) = γ2 0. For each triplet (κ, β0, γ0), we estimate the chance that complete separation does not occur (the MLE exists) by averaging over 50 i.i.d. replicates.

results.title: Are there any non-linear solutions of Cauchy's equation $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ without assuming the Axiom of Choice? - MathOverflow
results.content: # Are there any non-linear solutions of Cauchy's equation $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ without assuming the Axiom of Choice? It is also known that using an infinite dimensional basis for $\mathbb{R}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, it is possible *using the Axiom of Choice* to construct a function which is **not** linear. Yes, I probably should have been more clear, I actually wanted to ask whether: 1) it is possible to find an explicit expression for such a non-linear function (obvious answer: no, but I was interested in how to prove it isn't possible); 2) existence of solutions in ZF. The point is that it is consistent that every set of reals is measurable, and therefore every function $f:{\mathbb R}\to{\mathbb R}$ is measurable. The first to realize that it is possible using choice to construct a non-linear additive function was Hamel in 1905 (*Hamel, G.*, **Eine Basis aller Zahlen und die unstetigen Lösungen der Funktionalgleichung: (f(x+y) =f(x) +f(y)).**, Math. ZBL0207.00905.) proved that, relative to the consistency of an inaccessible cardinal, via forcing we can prove that it is consistent with ZF + DC that all sets of reals are Lebesgue measurable (DC is the axiom of dependent choice, a weak version of the axiom of choice useful to develop the basic theory of analysis). It follows that, in Solovay's model, all additive functions are linear and therefore no "explicit" example is possible. The two approaches are closely related: Assuming enough large cardinals, the inner model $L({\mathbb R})$ consisting of all sets constructible from reals *is* a model of determinacy, and a Solovay model. Let me close, however, by pointing out that, in appropriate models of set theory, we can "explicitly" build additive, non-linear maps. For example, in Gödel's inner model L of constructible sets, there is an easily definable Hamel basis (see this MO question), from which we can easily define such a function. $\begingroup$ A few links on Mathematics Stack Exchange about the result saying that measurable solutions of Cauchy functional equation are continuous: Show that $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ implies $f$ continuous $\Leftrightarrow$ $f$ measurable, Measurable Cauchy Function is Continuous, Prove that if a particular function is measurable, then its image is a rect line and Additivity + Measurability $\implies$ Continuity.

results.content: # Existence and non-existence results to a mixed anisotropic Schrödinger system in a plane Hajaiej, Rohit Kumar, Tuhina Mukherjee This article focuses on the existence and non-existence of solutions for the following system of local and nonlocal type − ∂ x x u + ( − Δ ) y s 1 u + u − u 2 s 1 − 1 = κ α h ( x , y ) u α − 1 v β in  R 2 , − ∂ x x v + ( − Δ ) y s 2 v + v − v 2 s 2 − 1 = κ β h ( x , y ) u α v β − 1 in  R 2 , u , v ⩾ 0 in  R 2 , where s 1 , s 2 ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) , α, β > 1, α + β ⩽ min { 2 s 1 , 2 s 2 }, and 2 s i = 2 ( 1 + s i ) 1 − s i , i = 1 , 2. The existence of a ground state solution entirely depends on the behaviour of the parameter κ > 0 and on the function h. In this article, we prove that a ground state solution exists in the subcritical case if κ is large enough and h satisfies (H). Further, if κ becomes very small, then there is no solution to our system. The study of the critical case, i.e., s 1 = s 2 = s, α + β = 2 s , is more complex, and the solution exists only for large κ and radial h satisfying (H1). Finally, we establish a Pohozaev identity which enables us to prove the non-existence results under some smooth assumptions on h. This paper demonstrates that a ground state solution exists for a mixed anisotropic Schrödinger system in a plane when is large enough and h satisfies (H1), but no solution exists if becomes very small. Title: Existence and non-existence results to a mixed anisotropic Schrödinger system in a plane - R Discovery
This study investigates the existence and non-existence of solutions for a mixed anisotropic Schrödinger system in the plane, showing that ground state solutions exist for large κ when h meets certain conditions, while solutions vanish as κ approaches zero; the critical case requires additional symmetry assumptions, and a Pohozaev identity is used to establish non-existence results under smoothness conditions on h. In this article, we prove that a ground state solution exists in the subcritical case if κ is large enough and h satisfies ( H ). More specifically, in the purely $$L^2$$ -subcritical case, we overcome the lack of compactness by virtue of the monotonicity of the least energy value and obtain the existence of ground state solution for $$\mu >0$$ . Precisely, motivated by Sirakov’s previous work, we prove some uniqueness results of positive (ground state) solutions for the special case \(\lambda \_1=\lambda \_2\). For the general case \(\lambda \_1\ne \lambda \_2\), we prove a sharp result on the parameter range for the existence of ground state solutions. We study the existence of ground state solutions for the following Schrödinger‐Poisson equations: urn:x-wiley:mma:media:mma4602:mma4602-math-0001 where is the sum of a periodic potential Vp and a localized potential Vloc and f satisfies the subcritical or critical growth. Although the Nehari‐type monotonicity assumption on f is not satisfied in the subcritical case, we obtain the existence of a ground state solution as a minimizer of the energy functional on Nehari manifold. The aim of this paper is to investigate the existence and asymptotic behavior of the solutions for the critical pseudo-relativistic Hartree equation $$ \sqrt{-\Delta+m^{2}}u+(\beta V(x)-\lambda)u =\bigg(\int\_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}\frac{|u(z)|^{2\_{\mu}^{\ast}}}{|x-z|^{\mu}}dz\bigg)|u| ^{2\_{\mu}^{\ast}-2}u $$% for $\mathbb{R}^{N}$, where $m, \lambda, \beta\in\mathbb{R}^+$, $0< \mu< N$, $N\geq3$, $2\_{\mu}^{\ast}=({2N-\mu})/({N-1})$ plays the role of critical exponent due to the Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality. By the way we also establish the existence and nonexistence results for the ground state solutions of the problems set on bounded domain.
